rationale: This mixed-methods case study (45 in-depth operator/official interviews, observations/GPS mapping, and n=292 random household surveys in three peri-urban settlements of Dar es Salaam) examines decentralized private self-supply and emerging informal water markets (propertization, commodification, and self-governance by independent self-help and market-oriented operators vs. public utility provision, alongside non-enforcement of commercial groundwater extraction permits under the Water Resources Management Act 2009 and municipal water quality certification, as well as unregulated private connection fees and unit prices). Thus regulatory_model_ownership is the dominant primary mechanism family. Empirically, the study evaluates how these governance arrangements shape both effective_access (reliability, proximity/distance, collection time, and water quality/waterborne illness) and economic_access (unit water prices and household water expenditure exceeding the 5% disposable-income affordability threshold) as co-central outcomes, making effective_access the primary outcome family and multiple the multi-outcome label.
